items.recommend_reason_zh: 文章用272个真实SFT任务对比：FLOP估算仅R²=0.31、MAE 12.41 h，仅用调度前信息的CatBoost达R²=0.98、MAE 1.71 h，解释微调为何常超FLOPs预期。

en.reason: Across 272 production SFT runs, FLOP-based estimates reached only R²=0.31 and 12.41 h MAE, while CatBoost using pre-scheduling information hit R²=0.98 and 1.71 h MAE, explaining why fine-tuning often outruns FLOP predictions.

en.title: Yuanzi: Surrounded by AI assistants — attention is at the center of everything
en.summary: After building 18 AI assistants, Yuanzi found himself overwhelmed by a constant flood of messages and to-dos — until it hit him: AI can handle execution at near-zero cost, but it can't replace the human cost of being present. He also shared a directly reusable attention-protection playbook: tiered task archiving, distilled personal preference guidelines, and strict daily limits on high-focus hours.

en.title: Sam Altman Makes Rare Remarks: I'm Not Worried About Anthropic Going Public First — There's No Shortage of Investors
en.summary:
I deeply empathize with Jensen Huang’s situation.

In an interview, Sam Altman addressed the AI industry’s core challenges: he stressed Jensen Huang’s irreplaceable role in AI development, warned that chip-capacity expectations may be overheated and that supply chains are lagging, and reiterated that humans must retain ultimate control over superintelligence. Chipmakers may be double-counting demand expectations; the DRAM shortage has exposed slow capacity expansion; OpenAI is uncompromising on human oversight and safety boundaries.

From whether Jensen Huang stays or leaves to compute investment in AI to whether superintelligence could cost humans control, Sam Altman discussed a range of key issues facing the AI industry in the latest interview. He expressed strong respect for Jensen Huang and deep empathy for his current situation, and said it is hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen. On rival Anthropic’s IPO this week, he said he is not worried about it going public first and believes AI still has huge capital and commercial room. He also warned that chipmakers’ demand expectations may be duplicated, and that the DRAM shortage exposes lagging supply-chain expansion. Facing public pushback against AI and data centers, he believes the industry must win back trust and explicitly commit that humans will always remain in control.
en.reason: Sam Altman said he is not worried about Anthropic going public first because the market still has plenty of investors, while warning that chipmakers may be double-counting demand and that DRAM shortages expose slow supply-chain expansion, and reaffirming OpenAI's commitment to human oversight.

en.title: Sam Altman Makes Rare Remarks: I'm Not Worried About Anthropic Going Public First — There's No Shortage of Investors
en.summary:
I deeply empathize with Jensen Huang’s situation.

In an interview, Sam Altman addressed the AI industry’s core challenges: he stressed Jensen Huang’s irreplaceable role in AI development, warned that chip-capacity expectations may be overheated and that supply chains are lagging, and reiterated that humans must retain ultimate control over superintelligence. Chipmakers may be double-counting demand expectations; the DRAM shortage has exposed slow capacity expansion; OpenAI is uncompromising on human oversight and safety boundaries.

From whether Jensen Huang stays or leaves to compute investment in AI to whether superintelligence could cost humans control, Sam Altman discussed a range of key issues facing the AI industry in the latest interview. He expressed strong respect for Jensen Huang and deep empathy for his current situation, and said it is hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen. On rival Anthropic’s IPO this week, he said he is not worried about it going public first and believes AI still has huge capital and commercial room. He also warned that chipmakers’ demand expectations may be duplicated, and that the DRAM shortage exposes lagging supply-chain expansion. Facing public pushback against AI and data centers, he believes the industry must win back trust and explicitly commit that humans will always remain in control.
en.reason: Sam Altman said he is not worried about Anthropic going public first because the market still has plenty of investors, while warning that chipmakers may be double-counting demand and that DRAM shortages expose slow supply-chain expansion, and reaffirming OpenAI's commitment to human oversight.
